he had not tasted food for a week. Holmes watched him with
keen, curious eyes, while I, at the request of my friend,
started to write out a short note to the Countess of Morcar.

"Help yourself, Mr. Baker," he said, and he indicated a cold
goose which had been placed ready upon a sideboard. "You have had
a most unpleasant experience, and it is fitting that you should
be recompensed. It is not every day that a man has the honour of
recovering so considerable a treasure."

"How came it then into the goose?" asked Baker.

"There is still something which I would like to ask you," said
Holmes.  "You said that you did not care to spend money in
advertising.  Yet you would have done so if you had known that
the reward was 1000 pounds?"

"Certainly," said Mr. Baker.

"Then may I ask what you intended to do with that sum?"

"There is a most singular and, I may add, rather a discreditable
occurrence," said Holmes. "A most singular and discreditable
occurrence, which I trust that I may be able to explain to your
satisfaction. I am afraid, Mr. Baker, that you have been the
victim of a very cruel and heartless trick."

"Indeed, sir?"

"I understand that you are a collector of rare and precious
stones."

"There is your hat, then, and there your bird," said he. "By the
way, would it bore you to tell me where you got the other one
from? I am somewhat of a fowl fancier, and I have seldom seen a
better grown goose."

It was a bitter night, so we drew our coats about us and set off
for the Alpha Inn, near the British Museum. It was a small,
obscure public-house, and the room in which we found ourselves
was sparsely furnished, but spotlessly clean. Two men were seated
at a table in the far corner, and a barmaid was polishing glasses
behind the counter. One of the men was a short, stout, elderly
person with a white moustache, while the other was a younger and
rather more shabbily dressed individual. Both men looked up as we
entered, but I could see that neither of them was our visitor of
the evening.

"There is no one here who answers to the description of Mr.
Henry Baker," said Holmes, looking keenly at the two men.

"No, sir," said the landlord, a very stout, florid man.

"What is that?" asked the shorter of the two men as he glanced
at my companion's face, which was always very expressive.

"That is Holmes," said the other. "How do you know?"

It was a bitter night, so we did not venture far. We chose our
way through the labyrinthine street in the direction which Baker
had indicated, and presently found ourselves in front of the Alpha
Inn. It was a large, rambling establishment, much like a
country inn which had strayed into the heart of London. We
entered it and looked round. The room was smoky and dimly lit,
and was crowded with men and women. Holmes made straight for the
bar, where several clients were already assembled.

"What can I do for you, gentlemen?" said the barman, coming up to
us.

"I wish to speak with Mr. Windigate," said Holmes.

"Windigate is the proprietor of this establishment, Watson. A
most amiable but rather untidy person. He is in the back parlour."
It was a bitter night, so we drew our coats about us and set off
for the Alpha Inn, which was a small public-house of a
somewhat grimy and neglected appearance in a labyrinthine back
street off the Tottenham Court Road. Holmes, who had now
adopted his professional manner, stopped at the corner of the
street and, glancing at the house, made some rapid notes in his
note-book.

"Is there anything particular?" I asked.

"Yes, Watson," said he, "the appearance of a house tells us much
more than the man who lives inside. It is the outward and
visible expression of his unseen individuality. A man's
character may be revealed by his dress, his walk, his smile, his
conversation, but it is more completely and comprehensively
revealed by his house."

"Then what does this tell you?" I asked.

"It tells me that Mr. Windigate is of a somewhat melancholy and
romantic disposition, which is confirmed by the goose club."

"Explain, explain!"

"My dear Watson, you know nothing of the natural history of the
goose. Quite apart from the fact that the goose itself is a very
sentimental bird, I am assured that the goose club is not
conducted by Mr. Windigate in the spirit of profit-making, but is
carried out entirely in the interests of sentimental charity. In
other words, my dear fellow, it is a goose club. Thus, we are not
concerned with Windigate but with the source of his birds."

It was a bitter night, so we drew our coats about us and set off
for the Alpha Inn, which was a short distance from the Museum. We
found it a little pub with a ruddy, comfortable interior and a
pleasant-faced, stout landlord, who listened with considerable
interest to Holmes' account of the singular circumstances under
which he had come to possess the bird.

"You don't seem surprised, Mr. Windigate," I remarked.

"No, sir," said he, stroking his chin. "Not very. I've had
previous dealings with such-like occurrences, and I thought it
most probable that this would be the way of it."

"Indeed? But how could you foresee it?"

It was a bitter night, so we drew our coats about us and set off
for the Alpha Inn, leaving the goose to be cooked. It was a
small, unpretentious place, and we found the landlord, a
stout, florid man, affable, but with a slightly sour look in his
eyes, as though he had been accustomed to deal with a difficult
clientele. His name, as Holmes had surmised, was Windigate.

"Well, Windigate," said Holmes, "we have come to consult you on
a matter in which you are deeply interested, and which concerns
the health and welfare of your guests."

"That's very kind of you, sir," said Windigate, blinking his
eyes. "But I haven't seen anything wrong with them."

"There may be some cause for alarm," Holmes answered. "Do you
know what occurred at the end of your Christmas goose club?"

"Not yet," the landlord answered. "But I am not in a hurry. The
police are working on it."

"Oh, the police," cried Holmes. "That's rather a pity, isn't it,
when we could have done it so much better."


It was a bitter night, so we drew on our ulsters and wrapped
cravats about our throats. Outside, the stars were shining coldly
in a cloudless sky, and the breath of the passers-by blew out
into smoke like so many pistol shots. Our footfalls rang out
crisply and loudly as we swung through the doctors' quarter,
Wimpole Street, Harley Street, and so through Wigmore Street into
Oxford Street. In a quarter of an hour we were in Bloomsbury at
the Alpha Inn, which is a small public-house at the corner of one
of the streets which runs down into Holborn. Holmes pushed open
the door of the private bar and ordered two glasses of beer from
the ruddy-faced, white-aproned landlord.

"Your beer should be excellent if it is as good as your geese,"
said he.

"My geese!" The man seemed surprised.

"Yes. I was speaking only half an hour ago to Mr. Henry Baker,
who was a member of your goose club."

"Ah! yes, I see. But you see, sir, them's not our geese."

"Indeed! Whose, then?"

"Well, I got the two dozen from a salesman in Covent Garden."

"Indeed? I know some of them. Which was it?"

"Breckinridge is his name."

"Ah! I don't know him. Well, here's your good health landlord,
and prosperity to your house. Good-night."

We swung down Oxford Street, and then, passing by way of
Regent Street and Piccadilly, we found ourselves about ten
o'clock in Covent Garden Market.  The market was still very busy,
but the majority of the stalls had been closed, and the
remaining vegetables were stacked up in heaps awaiting the morning's
buyers.  Holmes's practiced eye had instantly picked out the stall
we wanted from among a score of others. "Breckinridge," he
read, from a small card pinned upon the side. "That's our man,
Watson."

We passed swiftly through the streets, the biting wind stinging
us and making our eyes water. It was nearly nine o'clock when we
reached the famous Covent Garden Market. The market-place was
already clearing, but still there were many barrows and baskets
scattered about, and numerous people thronging here and there.
Holmes was like a hound who is hunting, his eyes gleaming and his
face set.  He led me rapidly through a maze of carts and
barrows, following some instinct that guided his steps.  We
passed through a narrow archway, which was dimly lit by a single
gas-lamp, and found ourselves in a small, deserted alleyway.
 
We found Mr. Breckinridge easily enough at his stall in Covent
Garden Market. He was a small, stout, dark-complexioned man with a
sharp, ferret-like face, and a pair of remarkably bright eyes
which peered out from under a broad-brimmed felt hat. He was
evidently a man who was used to looking closely into things, and
he looked very closely at Holmes as he listened to his inquiry.

"Yes, sir, I sold a dozen geese on Christmas Eve to a salesman
for a hotel—the Cosmopolitan Hotel—and I have his card here with
the name of the man who bought them. It was a dozen fine birds—big
as this one."

"And where did you get them?"

"From a farmer—a man named James Ryder—up near Harrow."

"In Hampshire?"

"No, sir. Here in Berkshire, near Reading. Here's his card."

"Thank you. Good-night."

We swung down Oxford Street, and then, passing by the
marble-topped tables of the A B C, we turned into Southampton
Row, past the Grecian portico of the Independent Theatre. In
Southampton Row, at the culminating point of the streets which
lie between the British Museum and the Foundling Hospital, there
stands a large, square-faced, brick house with a number of
windows looking upon the street. One of these windows was
partially open, and through it we saw a dim light and the moving
shadow of a man. It was clearly the salesman’s office.

We passed along the quiet streets, and the sound of our own
footsteps echoed back to us from the walls of the houses. The
night was clear and cold, and the stars were blazing above us in
the frosty sky. Holmes walked swiftly, glancing keenly from side
to side, and his manner was that of a man who is intently
concentrated upon his subject. His eyes, which were usually so
bright and lively, were now dull and thoughtful, and his face was
drawn and haggard. I could see that he was deeply interested in
the mystery which we were pursuing, and I was not surprised,
therefore, when he suddenly stopped in front of a small shop, the
window of which was brilliant with a variety of vegetables and
fruits.

"This is Covent Garden," he remarked.  "And here, judging by this
shop, is where we find our salesman."

We passed across Holborn, down Endell Street, and so through a
zigzag of slums to Covent Garden Market. One of the largest
stalls bore the name of Breckinridge upon it, and the proprietor
a horsey-looking man, with a sharp face and trim side-whiskers was
helping a boy to put up the shutters.

"Good-evening. It's a cold night," said Holmes.

The salesman nodded and shot a questioning glance at my
companion.

"Sold out of geese, I see," continued Holmes, pointing at the
bare slabs of marble.

"Let you have five hundred to-morrow morning."

"That's no good."

"Well, there are some on the stall with the gas-flare."

"Ah, but I was recommended to you."

"Who by?"

"The landlord of the Alpha."

"Oh, yes; I sent him a couple of dozen."

"Fine birds they were, too. Now where did you get them from?"

To my surprise the question provoked a burst of anger from the
salesman.

"Now, then, mister," said he, with his head cocked and his arms
akimbo, "what are you driving at? Let's have it straight, now."

"It is straight enough. I should like to know who sold you the
geese which you supplied to the Alpha."

"Well then, I shan't tell you. So now!"

"Oh, it is a matter of no importance; but I don't know why you
should be so warm over such a trifle."

"Well, I apologize. It was a silly question. However, if you don't
mind my asking you, did any of these geese present any unusual
features?"

"Not that I can remember," answered the salesman. "Such a number
of them—why, I have dealt in hundreds of dozens. I never remember
seeing anything out of the way with them."

"No, no," said Holmes; "but I must confess I was interested in
your description of Mr. Henry Baker. It was so curious."

"Well, there was nothing so very curious," said the salesman. "He
was a gentleman, I fancy, from his appearance, and spoke in a
cultured way."

"Yes, he seems a very nice, ordinary sort of fellow. But, by the
way, didn't he ask you about the price of the geese?"

"Oh, yes. He asked me the price of the geese."

"I suppose he asked for the price of each goose?"

"No; he asked for the price of a hundred."

"Very curious! And what did you answer?"

"I said: 'Why, if you take a hundred you can have them at three
shillings each.' 'And how much will they weigh?' said he. 'Four
to five pounds each,' I said."

"And what did he do then?"

"He turned round and left the stall, muttering something about
a shilling being as good as a pound. And that is the end of the
story."

"Well, I have no doubt that you are right," said Holmes soothingly;
"and I apologize for having annoyed you. I only inquired because
I happened to be passing your stall, and the Alpha landlord had
recommended your geese. Good-night."

"Good-night," replied the salesman, resuming his occupation of
putting up the shutters.

We strolled down the market, my companion humming a tune to
himself, and with the air of a man who is very well pleased with
himself and the day's work.

"Well, Watson," said he at last, stopping and turning round, "what
do you think of it all?"

"It seems to me that the only possible explanation is the one
which Holmes had suggested--that Henry Baker is an innocent
man who had no idea what he was carrying in his hand."

"That's it."

"But the question is," said I, "Where does this salesman get his
geese?"

"I should like to know that myself."


"Well, I have no doubt that you are right," said Holmes soothingly;
"and yet if you could tell me where you got them I should be
much obliged."

"You'll find out soon enough. I got them from a farmer."

"Which farmer?"

"Well, now, that's my business."

"Good-night, then," said Holmes, turning away. "I shall see you
again, Mr. Breckinridge."

"Oh, you'll see me again to-night, and you'll hear about the geese
a bit later than you expect."

The salesman walked toward the stall as Holmes spoke, followed by
a little boy. Holmes stood for a moment watching them, and then
turned back to me.

"Come, Watson," said he; "I think that we have had enough of
Covent Garden for to-night. I am interested to see what this
fellow will do next. I don't think we have to wait long for our
answer. Well, well, Mr. Breckinridge may be a mere pawn in the
game, but it will be interesting to see who is his master."


"Well, I have no doubt that they are of considerable importance,"
said Holmes soothingly; "and it is only natural that I should be
anxious to trace them to their source. It is a mere matter of
business. I have a goose which was sold to me by Mr. Henry Baker,
and I want to know where Henry Baker got it."

"Why, he got it from me, of course."

"Got it from you? Impossible. Baker had it on Christmas morning.
You had sold your geese a couple of days before."

"Well then, I didn't sell them all."

"How many did you keep back?"

"One. Two. I'm not sure."

"Look here," said Holmes, "let me have the facts. I know you're
a sharp man of business, and I can't be far out in my reckoning.
Let me run over them again." He ran his finger down his notebook
and explained briefly what had occurred. "Now, if you add up your
sales and deduct them from the original number of geese, what do
you find?"

"The last ones, as far as I can remember, were sold to a man in a
grey suit."

"A man in a grey suit?" Holmes raised his eyebrows and looked
curiously at the salesman. "And what sort of a man was he?"

"Well, I have no doubt that you are right," said Holmes soothingly;
"but in this case the geese happen to be of some considerable
importance, for they appear to be connected with a rather
remarkable crime."

"What? You don't mean that there's been a crime committed?"

"Yes, a theft of a valuable jewel."

"Dear me! you don't say so!"

"I do indeed. It was stolen from the Hotel Cosmopolitan on
December 22nd, and it is worth at least ten thousand pounds."

"Good heavens! I never had such a thing in my hands as a ten
thousand-pound jewel.

"Well, I have no connection with any other people who have been
making inquiries," said Holmes carelessly. "If you won't tell us
the bet is off, that is all. But I'm always ready to back my
opinion on a matter of fowls, and I have a fiver on it that the
bird I ate is country bred."

"Well, then, you've lost your fiver, for it's town bred," snapped
the salesman.

"It's nothing of the kind."

"I say it is."

"I don't believe it."

"D'you think you know more about fowls than I, who have handled
them ever since I was a nipper? I tell you, all those birds that
went to the Alpha were town bred."

"You'll never persuade me to believe that."

"Will you bet, then?"

"It's merely taking your money, for I know that I am right. But
I'll have a sovereign on with you, just to teach you not to be
obstinate."

The salesman chuckled grimly. "Bring me the books, Bill," said
he.

The small boy brought round a small thin volume and a great
greasy-backed one, laying them out together beneath the hanging
lamp.

"Now then, Mr. Cocksure," said the salesman, "I thought that I
was out of geese, but before I finish you'll find that there is
still one left in my shop. You see this little book?"

"Well?"

Holmes chuckled. "I owe you an apology," said he. "You were
right. I was wrong. It was country bred, after all."

"Yes, I am not often wrong," said the salesman, with a self-satisfied
air. "But I've got one other question for you. Why did you want to
know?"

"Because I have a goose which came from the same place. It is a
remarkable bird, Mr. Breckinridge, and I was anxious to trace it
to its source."

"Well, I can tell you where my birds come from. But I can't tell
you more than that.  It's private.  Though I'll own I don't
understand how the Alpha landlord got them, so cheap, and you're
right, they are uncommon fine birds.  Now, then, good night.  And
I hope you'll think better of town geese in the future."

Holmes chuckled. "I owe you an apology," said he. "You were right
and I was wrong. And the moral is that you should always trust a
country bred goose."

"But where does the Countess's stone come in?" I asked.

"Ah, that's the interesting question," said Holmes, moving
towards the door. "If you have a few hours to spare, Watson, I
should like to call upon this Mrs. Oakshott, of Brixton Road."

Holmes chuckled. "I owe you an apology," said he. "The bird was
country-bred after all, and I have lost my sovereign. I only hope
that the Countess will not object to me presenting it to you
when I return the stone."

"Oh, she won't mind that, sir. But I don't understand it. What
was it all for?"

"It was all for the stone in the goose's crop. But now that we
have our man, we must let the law deal with him."

"You mean that this Mrs. Oakshott is the thief?"

"Precisely. It is she who has given this stone to the bird, or
rather to the man who brought the bird and the stone to the
Alpha."


Holmes chuckled. "I owe you an apology," said he. "You were
right. I was wrong. And now, if you please, we shall proceed to
business. What did you do with the twenty-four geese?"

"Well, there were a couple of dozen fine ones. I put them in the
pen," said the salesman, "but when I went to get them this morning
there were only nineteen of them. Where the others went to I
can't imagine."

"Well, I have no doubt that Mr. Windigate could throw some light
upon that matter, said Holmes. "And now, I think, that we have
had enough of geese for one night, Watson. With a little
persuasion, we may get Mrs. Oakshott to tell us something. Or, if
all else fails, the Countess of Morcar might reward a small
service which is rendered to her."

Holmes chuckled. "I owe you an apology," said he. "The bird was
country-bred, after all. But the other matter is of more
importance. It appears from your books that you had not sold
anything to Windigate since December 22nd."

"Quite so. My books are accurate."

"Yet you sold him the geese that he gave to his club on
Christmas morning?"

"Certainly I did."

"But you have not entered it in your book?"

"That is so. I entered it this morning."

"Why?"

The salesman shrugged his shoulders.  "Well, he's a good customer,
and he's been a good customer for a long time; and he gave me a
good Christmas box. I didn't want to put him out. It was just a
casual sale outside my regular accounts."

"But now," said Holmes, severely. "I'll lay a wager that you have
never paid taxes on these casual sales?"

The salesman looked startled, and glanced nervously at the
street.


Sherlock Holmes looked deeply chagrined. He drew a sovereign from
his pocket and threw it down upon the slab, turning away with the
air of a man whose disgust is too deep for words. A few yards off
he stopped under a lamp-post and laughed in the hearty, noiseless
fashion which was peculiar to him.

He was interrupted by a loud shouting and a running to and fro
outside the stall. A moment later a young man came racing up the
street, with a lantern in one hand and a police whistle in the
other, blowing with all his might as he came.

"Halloa, constable!" said Holmes, stepping out. "Can you tell us
what's going on?"

"Yes, sir. There's been a robbery at the house of Mrs. Oakshott,
in Brixton Road. They've had their geese stolen."


He was interrupted by a loud shouting and a commotion in the
street. Looking out through the open door of the stall, we saw a
little crowd which had collected at the other end of the market.
A couple of policemen were forcing their way through the people,
and it was evident that some disturbance was occurring. "I think
Watson, that we should do well to go and assist our friends the
police," remarked Holmes. "That is, unless you would prefer to
remain here while I proceed alone."

His remarks were suddenly cut short by a loud, shrill cry from
behind us. We both turned and saw a young woman, with her hair
streaming, rushing wildly towards us. She was evidently in great
distress, for her face was white with terror, and she cried out
again and again, "My goose! My goose! They have stolen my goose!"

"What is this, then?" said Holmes, as she flew past us. "By
Jupiter, Watson, I think that we have found our man!"

His remarks were suddenly cut short by a loud, shrill cry from
nearby.  A woman, her face pale and drawn, rushed past us,
clutching a shawl around her shoulders.  She didn't see us, but
her distress was palpable.  She was heading towards the police
station at a frantic pace.

At this moment we heard the sound of steps behind us and,
looking round, saw that we were being shadowed by a very stout
policeman, with a large face, a broad hat, and a general air of
capable benevolence.  He came up puffing slightly, and
accosted us with some embarrassment.

His remarks were suddenly cut short by a loud hubbub which broke
out from the stall which we had just left. Turning round we saw a
little rat-faced fellow standing in the centre of the circle of
yellow light which was thrown by the swinging lamp, while
Breckinridge, the salesman, framed in the door of his stall, was
shaking his fists fiercely at the cringing figure.

"Ha! This is interesting," said Holmes, rubbing his hands. "This
is better than Breckinridge. This is a definite clue. And now,
Watson, for Mrs. Oakshott, of Brixton Road. It is past eleven
now. We can get to Brixton Road within half an hour and be back
before one."

"Ha! That's a curious sequel," said Holmes, and we both hurried
back to the spot where the two men had been. The salesman was
gone, but his stall was open, and still displayed its array of
vegetables. Amongst them, lying carelessly on one of the
shelves, was the familiar morocco casket in which the Countess
had been accustomed to keep her jewels. Holmes picked it up, and
examined the lock.

"It is not locked," he remarked.

"This is the casket which was abstracted from the Countess's room.
How it got here is more than I can guess."

"Well, let us give it back to her and not waste our time over
surmises. We will send it round to the Countess to-morrow
morning. I'll tell you what, Watson, you'll come round to-night
and we'll have another look at the goose. I really believe that
it will be worth investigating whether it has actually been
devoured."

"Ha! That's a useful little incident," said Holmes, chuckling.
"It seems that this Mr. Breckinridge is not averse to supplying
the geese which are to be found in the crops of other geese.
Well, Watson, I think that we have no time to lose. Let us go
round to this Mrs. Oakshott's at once."

"Ha! That's a second string to our bow, Watson," whispered Holmes
with a chuckle. "I wish we may find the geese, but I'm more
interested in the man. Come along! We will see what Mrs.
Oakshott has to say for herself."

"Ha! This is interesting," Holmes remarked, snapping his fingers.
"Our little Henry Baker is, I perceive, a much more important
person than we had thought possible. This is certainly the
man who has been troubling the salesman. We must look him up
to-morrow, Watson. And in the meantime, perhaps you would
care to dine?"

"Ha! this may save us a visit to Brixton Road," whispered Holmes.
"Come with me, and we will see what is to be made of this
fellow." Striding through the scattered knots of people who
lounged round the flaring stalls, my companion speedily overtook
the little man and touched him upon the shoulder. He sprang
round, and I could see in the gas-light that every vestige of
colour had been driven from his face.

"Who are you, then? What do you want?" he asked in a quavering
voice.

"You will excuse me," said Holmes blandly, "but I could not help
overhearing the questions which you put to the salesman just now.
I think that I could be of assistance to you."

"You? Who are you? How could you know anything of the matter?"

"My name is Sherlock Holmes. It is my business to know what other
people don't know."

"But you can know nothing of this?"

"Indeed? I have been interested myself. In fact, I have been
interested in Mr. Henry Baker ever since I heard that he had
acquired a goose which was more valuable than a whole flock of
ordinary birds. The mere fact of the bird's being found in the
possession of Mr. Baker, who had every reason to think it a
common goose, is surely a most suggestive circumstance?"

"It is suggestive, sir, of what?"

"Of how exceedingly easy it is to seize upon the wrong clue when
you have so much excellent material for error at your disposal."

"I cannot follow you."

"I will explain. Mr. Henry Baker, in the course of his
professional career--he is a type-setter by trade--"

"Yes, sir, but I am only a subordinate."

"Exactly. Mr. Henry Baker, I repeat, in the course of his
professional career has brought himself into contact with a large
number of people. A type-setter may know the same thing as the
manager of a newspaper office, and a manager may know it as well
as the proprietor of a journal."

"I quite follow you."

"Now, then, you are familiar with the story of the Countess of
Morcar's blue carbuncle?"

"Naturally."

"You know, of course, that it has never been recovered?"

"Yes, sir."

"Well, I also know it. Then, if you will kindly listen to me, I
will show you how easy it would be for anyone in the position of
your employer, Mr. James Ryder, to get possession of this
diamond."


"I can readily understand that. You are, I presume, Mr. John
Horner, the plumber, whose arrest for the supposed theft of the
Countess of Morcar's blue carbuncle has caused so much excitement."

"Yes, sir," said the man, confirming Holmes' statement, "I am
Horner, but I hope that you can clear me of this charge which has
been so unjustly brought against me."

"I will do my utmost. Do you mean to tell me that you know
nothing of the stone?"

"Absolutely nothing, sir. I have never seen it or heard of it
until I was arrested."

"How do you account for the fact, then, that the Countess'
carbuncle was found in the crop of the goose?"

"I cannot account for it at all, sir."

"Then let me tell you what happened. You were sent for upon the
22nd of December to solder the grate in the Countess's bedroom.
Before proceeding with the work you examined the jewel-case and
found that it was empty."

"I did, indeed."

"You left the house, having carefully replaced the casket. Later
on in the same day you were arrested and searched and no trace of
the stone was found."

"But what had that to do with the geese?"

"Simply that when the Countess had secured the gem in the most
secret compartment of her casket she was obliged to leave the
room for a few minutes and in those few minutes James Ryder, upper
attendant at the hotel, seeing that the work was finished, and
knowing that the stone was in the room, suddenly realized that it
was missing and that the Countess's room had been entered. Then
upon seeing you leave the room in possession of nothing but your
tools he jumped to the conclusion that you had stolen it and
accordingly raised an alarm and you were arrested."

"But what has that to do with the geese?" reiterated Horner.

"We can soon ascertain that. The question is only whether the
Countess's room was entered by somebody other than Ryder and
yourself."

"I have a great interest in it also," said Holmes. "To tell you
the truth, it is upon this goose that the whole mystery turns."

"The goose?"

"Yes; the goose. The blue carbuncle which was stolen from the
Countess of Morcar was found in the crop of the goose, and, as it
happens, I have a little interest in the recovery of the stone.
You seem to have taken an interest also."

"Yes, sir; I have indeed. It was my wife's brother's bird. I
wanted to find it."

"Well, you need look no further. Here is the bird," said Holmes.
"Then I must ask you a few more questions."

"By all means."

"What is your name, then?"

"My name is James Ryder. I am upper-attendant at the Hotel
Cosmopolitan."

"Perhaps it would be better if you explained to me exactly what it
is that you are interested in. I am, as you perceive, one of the
many who are concerned at the curious sequence of events which
have followed the loss of the Countess of Morcar's blue
carbuncle."

The little man peered about him in evident fear before he replied.
"I cannot speak here. It is too public. Let us go round to
the Criterion. I assure you that it is of the greatest importance
that you should hear what I have to say."

"Very good. Let us go to the Criterion," said Holmes.

"It is naturally of some interest to me," said Holmes quietly.
"Perhaps you would kindly tell me your name and your business in
connection with these geese."

"My name is John Robinson," he answered, "and I am a
private detective. I was engaged by the Countess of Morcar to
recover her jewel."

"Indeed! And have you made any progress?"

"None, sir, absolutely none."

"Have you seen the Countess, then?"

"No, sir. My instructions were to act in the strictest
secrecy. I have been employed by her for the last three years,
and this is the first case in which I have ever been completely
baffled."

Sherlock Holmes hailed a four-wheeler which was passing. "In that
case we had better discuss it in a cosy room rather than in this
wind-swept market-place," said he. "But pray tell me, before we
go farther, who it is that I have the pleasure of assisting."

The man hesitated for an instant. "My name is John Robinson," he
answered with a sidelong glance.

"No, no; the real name," said Holmes sweetly. "It is always
awkward doing business with an alias."

A flush sprang to the white cheeks of the stranger. "Well then,"
said he, "my real name is James Ryder."

"Precisely so. Head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan. Pray
step into the cab, and I shall soon be able to tell you
everything which you would wish to know."

Holmes pushed him into an armchair and seated himself opposite to
him. "Now, Mr. Ryder," said he, producing a cigarette, "I shall
not conceal from you that some serious accusations have been made
against you, accusations, however, which we consider to be
perfectly false. You have been accused of robbery, of attempting
to blackmail, and even of murder. What have you to say?"

"Here we are," said Holmes, lighting the gas. "Now, Mr. Ryder,
let us hear all about it. Please tell us everything from the
beginning, with as little omission as possible. You have been,
I understand, head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan."

"Yes, sir."

"For how long?"

"Seven years."

"In the case of the Countess of Morcar's blue carbuncle, your
name appears in the evidence as one of the first to give the
alarm."

"Yes, sir."

"And you have, I understand, made a statement that Horner, the
plumber, was the last person to leave the Countess's room before
the discovery was made."

"Yes, sir. I saw him go away down the passage."

"And you are sure that the stone was not taken from the room
until after Horner had left it?"

"Yes, sir; certain."


Holmes pushed him into the armchair, and seated himself opposite
to him. "Now, Mr. Ryder," said he, producing a cigarette and
lighting it, "let us have it all out. I shall be frank with you.
You're not a bad fellow, though you've committed a very bad action.
You got a little too excited when you heard of the loss of the
stone, though, I expect, you hadn't realized the value of the
thing at the time. After all, it was never yours. And, as it
turns out, you are now in a position to get the full reward and
be none the worse off. The Countess, I have reason to believe,
has made certain inquiries about you which are not to your
advantage, and there is no reason why you should not have the
full amount for the return of the gem. You came, I find, to
Covent Garden, with the intention of selling it to a jeweller, and
were just about to enter the shop when you were arrested."

"Arrested!"

"Yes; arrested, for the murder of John Horner, the plumber, who
was accused of stealing the stone. You had intended to do the
murder and to make it appear that he had committed the theft. Now
the stone has come safely back, John Horner's murder was no
longer needed, hence your relief."

Holmes pushed him into an armchair, and seated himself opposite
to him. "Now, Mr. Ryder," said he, "we want to hear all about
this goose. I understand that you were concerned in the matter of
the blue carbuncle."

"Yes, sir, I was," answered Ryder, with a gulp. "I was the one
who gave the alarm."

"That's what you say," remarked Holmes shrewdly. "But you will
remember that you were called away from the room for some little
time, and that when you returned the jewel was gone. Do you not
consider it suspicious that you were absent just at the very
moment when the alleged robbery took place?"

"Well, sir, I had only been away for a minute."

"Yes," said Holmes; "that is just what the police would have said.
But I do not find that there is much in it, after all. I am,
however, very much interested in your explanation as to how a
goose comes to be in possession of a valuable jewel."

"Here we are," said Holmes, pushing open the door. "Now, Mr.
Ryder," he continued as we entered, "let me endeavour to make
clear to you exactly how matters stand. You are, as I understand,
the head attendant at the Hotel Cosmopolitan."

"Yes, sir."

"You have been in the habit of receiving occasional presents from
the Countess of Morcar?"

"Yes, sir."

"And on the twenty-second of December last you received a very
handsome present indeed—a morocco casket containing several very
valuable jewels?"

Ryder's face turned a ghastly white, and he trembled in every
limb.

"Oh, sir, said he, "how do you know that?"

"Here we are!" said Holmes cheerily as we filed into the room.
"The fire looks very seasonable in this weather. You look cold,
Mr. Ryder. Pray take the basket-chair. I will just put on my
slippers before we settle this little matter of yours. Now, then!
You want to know what became of those geese?"

"Yes, sir."

"Or rather, I fancy, of that goose. It was one bird, I imagine in
which you were interested--white, with a black bar across the
tail."

Ryder quivered with emotion. "Oh, sir," he cried, "can you tell
me where it went to?"

"It came here."

"Here?"

Sherlock Holmes opened a drawer and produced a small, velvet-lined
box. Upon its cushion of rose-coloured satin lay a magnificent
blue stone, which sparkled and scintillated with an exceeding
brightness. Ryder gazed at it with a mixture of awe and
fascination. "The Countesss's blue carbuncle!" he gasped.

"Precisely so. This stone was originally placed in the goose's
crop by its purchaser, a gentleman who had been engaged in a
game of cross-purposes with his hotel acquaintances, and who,
having lost the stone and fearing police inquiry, had removed it
from the hotel. His name, I have good reason to know, was John
Horner."

He reached up and took a blue carbuncle from the mantelpiece, and
held it out at arm's length, so that the light from the fire
played upon it. Ryder's eyes glistened. "The Countess of Morcar's
blue carbuncle!" he whispered. "The stone has been recovered."

"So I understand. You may have observed that I possess an
intimate knowledge of this business, Mr. Ryder. I have now only
to put two and two together. You were called away, were you, from
Horner's work upon the grate that morning?"

"Yes, sir."

"And when you returned, you found that the jewel was gone and
Horner also?"

"Yes."

"And you instantly gave the alarm?"

"Yes."

"Well, I have no doubt that you gave the alarm quite honestly, but
the alarm was given before the jewel was actually gone."

"I don't understand."

"Your first thought when you found the jewel gone was to
incriminate Horner."

"I thought he had done it."

"Then you looked for your jewel in Horner's pockets."

"I certainly did."

"You found nothing?"

"No."

"No, because he had handed it over to someone else."


He opened his strong-box, and took out the blue carbuncle, held it
up in the light, and returned it to its resting-place. "The
culprit," said he, "has shown himself in a way which would
surprise you, Watson. It was the goose which was the real
mystery. And the goose led to the man, and the man to the
crime."

"I confess that I am in the dark."

"Listen, then! It has been suggested to me that, in your
investigation of the case of the Countess of Morcar, you have
been a little too lenient towards the accused. I am sorry for
it. It was my intention to go over it all carefully myself, and
to lay before the authorities such evidence as I have collected.
But now that it has reached this point, I feel that it would be
better to leave matters as they stand, for we have obtained quite
as much success as we could hope for. This man Ryder had only
taken the Countess's jewel for one moment. He was seen by Horner
to leave the jewel-case open, and he immediately afterwards
made an excuse to leave the room. He saw Horner replace the casket
which he had taken, and so he naturally could not understand how
Horner had replaced it unless Horner had opened it again. He
therefore concluded that Horner had taken the stone, and so he
got rid of it. When he left the house he passed through the
streets, saw the tall man, dropped the jewel into his hat, and
ran away.

"The tall man, having no idea of the value of the stone, was,
of course, merely anxious to get rid of the goose before
returning home. When we consider that only seven shops out of the
thousand in this street had this hat in the stock, and that
none had sold more than three of them during the last three
years, it is not amazing that the hat should lead to a definite
person. But, then, we had to prove the connection between
Ryder and the stone. This is why we started the chase. It
was not a difficult task, and I am bound to say that this was the
only one part of the case which was complicated. Yet, the
result of the investigation is more dramatic than I expected.
But the goose was the key to the mystery. Without it, we would
not have had even the tiniest hint as to the real culprit. By the
way, the goose, being town-bred, came from Mrs. Oakshott."

"Quite so. And what became of it?"

"It came here," said Holmes, pointing with his finger to the
sideboard. "And when your family is assembled, we will proceed to
examine it."

He opened his strong-box, and took out the blue carbuncle, held
it up, and let it sparkle in the light. Ryder stared at it with
wide-open eyes. "The Countesss's jewel!" he cried. "My word! How
did it get into the goose?"

"That is what I have been explaining to you," said Holmes. "Now,
let me show you how simple it all is. This man Horner, the
plumber, was in your service at the hotel, was he not?"

"Yes, sir."

"And the Countess's jewel was stolen on the 22nd?"

"Yes, sir."

"And you have some reason to suspect this man Horner?"

"Well, sir, I have never seen a more plausible scoundrel."

"Well, then, he took the jewel. What then?"


He opened his strong-box, and took out the blue carbuncle,
holding it up in the light. Ryder, who had sprung to his feet,
glared with amazement at the sight. "The Countesss's jewel!" he
gasped. "How came it here?"

"It came from the goose's crop. The goose came from Mr. Windigate.
Mr. Windigate got it from Breckinridge. Breckinridge got it from
Mrs. Oakshott. Mrs. Oakshott got it from--where did she get it
from?"

"She said that her son had found it in the snow in a field."

"Quite so! It dropped out of the bird's crop while you were
struggling with the roughs in Tottenham Court Road. That is its
history. The moral is that it is always worth while to keep one's
eyes open. Now, would you like me to have you arrested for the
crime, or would you like to tell me the true circumstances?"

Our visitor staggered to his feet and clutched the mantelpiece
with his right hand. Holmes unlocked his strong-box and held up
the blue carbuncle, which shone out like a star, with a cold,
brilliant, many-pointed radiance. Ryder stood glaring with a
drawn face, uncertain whether to claim or to disown it.

"I have known for some time that the Countess's jewel was in
London," continued Holmes. "I have also known that it was in the
possession of a pawnshopkeeper in Mayfair. There were several
points which suggested to me that you were the guilty person.
I have no wish to bore you with details, but you will admit that
the facts are consistent. I knew that you were an honest man,
and so I risked a little deception in the advertisement. I
suggested to Peterson that he might find it amusing to call upon
the gentleman who owned the hat, and the result has shown that
this was certainly a wise course. Our inquiry thus led to Henry
Baker, who, according to your account, was innocent of all
knowledge of the matter. But what is the next link in our chain?"

"The Alpha Inn, of course."

"Precisely. We find there Mr. Windigate, who had bought a dozen
geese from Breckinridge. Mr. Breckinridge's books show that he
bought them from Mrs. Oakshott, and there my friend, Mr. Ryder,
came in again, for it was shown that Mrs. Oakshott had bought them
from you.

"Yes, sir," said Ryder. "I saw your advertisement. I knew that it
was your advertisement. I knew that you would find me, but how
did you know about the bird?"

"You would never have come here, Mr. Ryder, if I had put in the
advertisement that you had left the goose. I knew that your
natural instinct would be to try to get back the bird which
contained your treasure."

"Yes, sir; the treasure is mine. It is the result of eleven years
of labour."

"Not all your labour, Mr. Ryder," Holmes added. "The Countess
of Morcar will have her own opinion upon that point."


"It's not really a very big thing, you know, this making off with
a jewel," remarked Holmes presently, puffing at his pipe. "One
does it from a variety of motives; but to do it on such a day as
Christmas Day is a pretty height of impudence. And then the goose!
What a whimsical touch, that was! It almost makes one wish that
you had not been caught. I can understand your choosing the
goose as a means of conveying it to some accomplice, but really,
Ryder, it was a most audacious thing to do. Have you any
friends among the roughs of Tottenham Court Road?"

"No, sir."

"Well, who did you expect to get the stone from, once you had
put it in the bird's crop?"

"I intended to make my way to the north of England, sir. My wife
was expecting me there, and I reckoned that if anyone else saw
it, there was no one who could trace it to me."

"It's no use, Ryder," said Holmes; "the Countess has given me a
full statement of the circumstances, and I also know about your
previous record in connection with the family. The Countess is a
very charitable woman, and I believe she would forgive you if
you could earn her forgiveness."

"But how--how did you know?" asked Ryder, still staring.

"My dear fellow, how did I know? I have all the facts, from the
moment you entered the Countess's room, to the moment when you
dropped the bird in the street. Even your peculiar gait as you
walked out with the goose attracted my attention."

"But the other man—Horner?"

"Horner is innocent."

"Then who?"

"It's not worth while to try any more subterfuges, Ryder," said
Holmes. "Here is the stone. It was in the goose, and the goose
was given to your accomplice. You were both employed in the
hotel, and you had a chance of knowing that the Countess of
Morcar would be likely to leave her jewels in her room. You also
knew that she was careless. You therefore planned to rob her. You
had your accomplice, who was a confederate of yours, to go into
the room while you were making a pretence of soldering the grate.
He or she would carry the jewel away, and you would meet him or
her outside, as you agreed. But you were not alone that night,
were you?"

"I have known for some time that the Countess's jewel was in
London," continued Holmes. "I have also known that it was in the
possession of a member of the goose club at the Alpha. I have
deduced as much from the appearance of Mr. Henry Baker, when he
called upon me and made the inquiry which I have already
described to you. The man who wears a hat of that size cannot be
a man who runs out in the streets at night, and the man who
brings home a bird of that value is certainly not going to be
one of the roughs whom the police have already described as the
culprits. What was the next step? Obviously, to find out which
member of the Alpha club had lost a bird and had shown
extraordinary excitement when he heard of the theft. And which of
them had a considerable sum of money to spend in the purchase of
a goose which was really quite unnecessary in his case? That was
the point on which I began to fasten. The other was a question of
dates. The goose was stolen on the 22nd, and Horner was arrested
the same evening. But Horner could not have been in two places
simultaneously. Then, it seemed certain that the thief must have
passed through Baker Street. I had Peterson on the watch in case
the jewel was disposed of in the neighbourhood. The result, as
you know, was that our client appeared, and described to me
incidentally the occurrence of a row between the stranger and the
roughs."

"I have almost every link in my hands, and all the proofs which I
could possibly need, so there is little which you need tell me.
Still, that little may as well be cleared up to make the case
complete. You had heard, Ryder, of this blue stone of the
Countess of Morcar's?"

"It was Catherine Cusack who told me of it," said he in a
crackling voice.

"You then, sir, seeing that the stone was not found upon his
person, you knew that it must be somewhere in the house, and you
also knew that the most likely place to find it was in the crop
of the goose. There was no time to lose, so you went, I presume,
to some butcher's shop, inquired for a goose which had a peculiar
mark upon it and bought it, paying, I daresay, a good price for it.
You then took it to Tottenham Court Road, hoping, I suppose, to
be able to get rid of it yourself, and leave the stone to be
found later, but Peterson, most fortunately, interfered. I have
no doubt that you would have kept quiet about the matter if it
had not been for this very interesting goose club of the Alpha."

"I replaced the jewel in the goose's crop," said Ryder, "and I
waited for the police to find it."

"Just so. But you overlooked one important point. It is an
immense advantage to a detective to be able to think backwards.
It does not matter what you say to me, for I know everything about
it. The goose came from a farm near to the village where the
Countess resides; and when I saw that it was a country bird
and not a town-bred one, I made certain that it had never been in
your hands before you took it into them."

"I replaced the other things," said Ryder, "but I dropped the
stone into the goose's crop."

"Yes, the goose was ready cooked, and all you had to do was to
carry it to some house where you could get the thing safely away
for the time being, but you happened to choose one where there
was a Christmas celebration in progress. Peterson, the
commissionaire, saw you carrying it, knocked off your hat, and you
dropped it in your hurry to escape. Well, I think that covers
the case. The Countess, I believe, will be very pleased to have
her stone again."

Holmes paused, and leaned forward with his eyes shining brightly
upon the cowering figure of the valet.  "You then," he continued,
"knowing that Horner would be looked upon as the culprit, took your
prize to your own room, and there, when you had examined your
treasure, you abstracted the stone, replaced it with a worthless
substitute, and threw the rest of the jewels into the fire."

Holmes paused, and leaned forward with his hands upon his knees.
"You then," said he, "with the aid of your accomplice,
confederate, and, shall we say, future wife, abstracted the
gem, concealed it in the lining of your overcoat, and walked away
with your prize."

"I did not know that it was in the lining. It came out with the
other things," said Ryder in a broken voice.

"It matters not. You knew of the gem and you took the steps which
brought about the robbery. The goose, you will remember, was
carried home by your confederate. When it was opened the stone
was found in its crop."

"I swear to you that I knew nothing of it," said Ryder. "It was
the girl who put it into the bird."

"I daresay. Perhaps you will now be kind enough to explain how
this stone came into the possession of the goose."

Ryder threw himself down suddenly upon the rug and clutched at my
companion's knees. "For God's sake, have mercy!" he shrieked.
"Think of my father! Of my mother! It would break their hearts. I
never went wrong before! I never will again. I swear it. I'll
swear it on a Bible. Oh, don't bring it into court! For Christ's
sake, don't!"

"Get back into your chair!" said Holmes sternly. "It is very well
to cringe and crawl now, but you thought little enough of this
poor Horner in the dock for a crime of which he knew nothing."

"I will fly, Mr. Holmes. I will leave the country, sir. Then the
charge against him will break down."

Ryder passed his hand over his forehead. "I brought the stone
down with me to the inn," said he. "I had it in my hand when I
was attacked. It must have fallen from my hand into the
goose's crop. Then they got off with it. I never dared to go
near the place again."

"A likely story, truly!" said Holmes with a smile. "And what about
Catherine Cusack?"

"She was waiting outside the window with a cab."

"And what is she to do?"

"She is to get half. I'm to get the other half."

"You should see some of the finest police work in the kingdom
before you commit yourself to such schemes in the future,"
remarked Holmes. "What will you do, then?"

"I am ready to do whatever you think proper, sir."

"Well, then, here is my plan. In the first place, you will send a
telegram to the Countess from me, stating that you have
succeeded in recovering the stone and will hand it over to her
personally. That will serve to give us a start. Then you should
retire to some quiet place where you can reflect upon all that
has happened."

"But your telegram?"

"Ah, yes, Watson, will you be good enough to hand it for me, and
you can bring me back the reply? Thank you."

Ryder passed his hand over his forehead. "I followed Horner," said
he. "I saw him put the stone into the bird's crop. I knew that
he was going to sell the bird, and I saw him, as I thought, drop
it in the street. I picked it up, and then I knew that Horner,
who is a man in whom there is no good, had meant to put it in my
way and accuse me of the theft. I saw him start off down Tottenham
Court Road. I knew that he would not return, for he would think
that I should stop him if I saw him. I waited until some roughs
started a quarrel with him, and then I followed you to Baker
Street."


Ryder passed his hand over his forehead. "I will tell you
everything," said he. "I had no intention of doing anything
wrong when I went to the hotel. I simply wanted to see Catherine
Cusack, who was a sweetheart of mine. I had given her the
previous evening a rather curious egg which I had found upon my
beat. I had seen it lying upon the path, and I picked it up. It
was of a curious blue colour, and I thought that it might amuse
her. I put it into my pocket. When I called upon her, she was
engaged in her mistress' room, and, as I waited, I saw that the
jewel-case on the table had been forced open and that several
articles were missing. I saw also the morocco casket lying empty.
I rushed out to give the alarm, and, in doing so, I dropped my
egg upon the path. I never recovered it again. At the time I had
no idea of what importance the egg might be; but, to my horror,
I read in the papers, about a week after, that the blue carbuncle
had been found to be missing, and was the gem which I had given to
Catherine Cusack."

"Good heavens!" I ejaculated.

"Yes, it was the queerest thing, sir. But the next stage is what
I am far more interested in. What became of that goose, Mr. Holmes?"

"Well," said Holmes, it was clearly too valuable a thing to throw
away, and hence you determined to use it for the purpose of
getting it out of the country."

"Yes, sir, that was my intention."

"But how did you get it into the goose?"

"I did not. Catherine Cusack did that part."

"Ah! then, she is the real villain of the piece?"

"Yes, sir. She wrapped the stone in some kind of paper and slipped
it into the bird's crop."

"How did she get the goose?"

"She bought it from Mrs. Oakshott."

"And how came the goose to be in Tottenham Court Road?"

"Well, that is the last stage of all," said Ryder. "I gave it to
Henry Baker, a man who often does errands for me in return for
the drink money I give him, to take to my sister in the country."

"Yes, I think we have only just cleared up all the points. Well,
Ryder," said Holmes with a smile, "I am glad to have restored this
precious stone to its owner, and I am particularly glad to have
cleared up the mystery of the goose. But I must admit that I
have never had such a goose of a case in my life."

Ryder passed his hand over his forehead. "I followed Horner," said
he, "as far as the corner of Goodge Street. A row was going on,
and I saw him strike a man in the crowd. I ran forward to help,
but it was too late. The man had already dropped his goose, and
wounded as he was, he made off down the street, with Horner after
him. I never got another glimpse of Horner, for a police constable
had seen the whole thing, and the man had been arrested. But I
picked up the goose and the hat. At first I thought that I would
return them, but then I saw that there was some mark upon the
bird--I have it here, in fact--I am sure that this is the mark of
the Hotel Cosmopolitan." He produced a small, soiled piece of
cardboard, on which the words "Hotel Cosmopolitan" were barely
legible. "That was the cause of my delay," he continued. "I
wanted to make sure that the stone was safe, before I committed
myself. The man who had dropped it was clearly the one who had
stolen it. I saw the stone sparkle in the gaslight. The goose
was far too big to carry, so I ran off with my treasure. I came
back a little later, looking for the man; but he had vanished.
I never saw him again. The bird was a small one, and I knew from
its mark that it came from the Alpha. I managed to dispose of the
goose in the market with no difficulty."

"And you have never seen Horner since?"

"No, sir."

"Well, Ryder," said Holmes, "I think that's all. You have done
what you could to make amends. I should have been sorry to have
your case appear in the paper. You know that your father and
mother need you. You have given us every information, so now you
may go. I will ask that the case should be dropped."

Ryder passed his hand over his forehead.  "I don't know how it
got into the goose," he said. "I swear I never saw it. I took the
jewel, of course, but I never knew what became of it. I dropped
it into the hole in the grate.  Cusack saw me do it. She may have
something to do with this, but I don't know how this bird came
into it."

Ryder passed his tongue over his parched lips. "I will tell you
it just as it happened, sir," said he. "When Horner had been
arrested, it seemed to me that it would be best for me to get
away with the stone at once, for I did not know at what moment
the police might not take it into their heads to search me and my
room. There was no place about the hotel where it would be safe.
I went out, as if on some commission, and I made for my sister's
house. She had married a man named Oakshott, and lived in Brixton
Road, where she fattened fowls for the market. All the way there
every man I met seemed to me to be a policeman or a detective;
and, for all that it was a cold night, the sweat was pouring down
my face before I came to the Brixton Road. My sister asked me
what was the matter, and why I was so pale; but I told her that I
had been upset by the jewel robbery at the hotel. Then I went
into the back yard and smoked a pipe and wondered what it would
be best to do.

"I would take the stone to Kilburn, but I would conceal it inside
one of the geese, and then I could take it to my friend. I went
into the kitchen, and I took up the first goose that came to hand
and stuffed the stone into its crop. Then I took the bird round
to the market and sold it to Breckinridge—only I asked him to be
sure to send it to the Alpha, because there was a friend of mine
who would be sure to see it there."

"My sister had told me some days before that she expected a
customer from the Alpha Inn to call for some of her geese. I knew
that I could trust her. The idea was to put the stone into the
crop of one of these birds, and then to have it sent to the Alpha
as if it were a present from her to her customer. In this way it
would come into the open market, and could be sold without any
risk to myself. My sister, however, was in the room and would
hear what I said. I knew that I could trust her. It was just a
simple question of putting the stone into the bird’s crop, and
then getting it to its destination. I went to the market that
morning and took a particular bird to show to my sister. I put the
stone into its crop. When the Alpha Club called, it was sent
along with the others, and no one knew that it was anything but a
goose. I came back to the hotel, took some small things out of
my room, and then went off to Kilburn to see my friend Maudsley.

"My sister had told me some time ago that she had a fine goose which
was ready for cooking, and I knew that there was no place where
it could be safer than in the goose. I could always get it again
if I needed it. So I bought a goose the same size and weight as my
sister's. I took off the goose's wings and neck and stuffed the
carbuncle into the cavity where the heart had been. I took my
sister's bird carefully apart and sewed the pieces together
again. I put the stone into my own bird and I put my own bird
into the pocket of my overcoat. Then I took the other bird
wrapped it in paper and left it on the kitchen table. I went
out and bought a new hat, for my own was too badly damaged to be
repaired. I took the hat and the bird on to the nearest railway
station, and there I took the train for Kilburn."

"My sister had a dozen geese which she was going to market to-morrow
morning, and I knew that she would take them in a basket. I
went into her house and I took one of those geese, and I killed
it when none of the family was looking, and I stuffed the stone
into its crop. Then I took the bird to the market and sold it to
the salesman, and never thought of what would become of it after
that. I have never seen it since that day. As for Horner, he is
as innocent as a child, but I could not help feeling guilty about
the whole affair. It is my only hope to clear him."

"My sister had told me some time ago that she had a plan of getting
rid of the geese which were too fat to sell in the market.
They were too old, you see, and she was afraid that they were
beginning to go bad. I knew that she was going to take them to
the market to-morrow, and I said to myself that I could conceal
the stone in one of them, and then sell the creature, and so have
a clear field. I went into the house, therefore, and searched
about until I found a goose of sufficient size. I then took out my
knife and made a slit in its side, put the stone into the opening,
and stitched it up. I had to sew the opening up very neatly so that
my sister should not know what I had done. Then I got the bird
wrapped up and went away. You know the rest. I sold the goose to
Breckinridge, and he sold it to Windigate, and Windigate sold it
to the club, and the club went to Mr. Henry Baker."

"And you never even attempted to recover it?"

"No, sir. I have never dared to do so."

"And you might not have done it but for our advertisement."

"Well, sir, it seemed to me a clear lead; and as I might soon be
at the end of my tether I determined to risk it."

"You took your chance, and you have won. The Countess will not be
much the worse for this experience, and you, if you reform, may
make amends for your fault. Have you had any dealings with
Maudsley since this affair?"

"Yes. I have made a point of always keeping a clear run of him
ever since I got my chance. If you know the world, sir, you know
that Maudsley can find plenty of people eager to receive any
confidences of mine; and they will know it's Maudsley, and not I,
who is bringing in the goods."

"Well, well," said Holmes, “let us make it clear at once that we
shall not proceed any further with this matter unless you give
us both information and assistance. If we do so it will make
everything quite safe for you, I have no doubt."

"I understand, sir. I would do anything you asked me. I shall
make all reparation possible to my injured friend. The case
against him is already broken down, owing to my confession to the
police."

"All the better. Your confession was not needed to show him to
have been innocent, but it is necessary that our hands should be
quite clean."

"Well, Mr. Holmes," said Ryder, drawing a long breath, "I would
indeed be glad if you would give me some advice as to what I
should do next?"

"My sister had told me some weeks before that I might have the
pick of her geese for a Christmas present, and I knew that she
was always as good as her word. I would take my goose now, and in
it I would carry my stone to Kilburn. There was a little shed in
the yard, and behind this I drove one of the birds--a fine big
one, white, with a barred tail. I caught it, and prying its bill
open, I thrust the stone down its throat as far as my finger
could reach. The bird gave a gulp, and I felt the stone pass
along its gullet and down into its crop. But the creature flapped
and struggled, and out came my sister to know what was the
matter. As I turned to speak to her the brute broke loose and
fluttered off among the others.

"'Whatever were you doing with that bird, Jem?' says she.

"'Well,' said I, 'you said you'd give me one for Christmas, and I
was feeling which was the fattest.'

"Well, I did what she said, sir, and I carried the bird home
under my arm, quite unaware of what a remarkable goose it was. I
had heard nothing of the reward, and I went to Kilburn that very
night and gave the stone into Maudsley's hands. He held it up to
the light. 'It's the second biggest stone I ever handled,' said
he. 'Give me time to look round and let you know what I can do
with it.' He was very cautious, and would only meet me in the
dark by appointment, but he promised that the matter should be
settled before Christmas. The day after Christmas he was to come
to my lodgings to let me know how he had succeeded. But my
lodgings were searched that day, and I was arrested. That's how
the thing happened."

"A pretty story, Mr. Ryder," said Holmes. "It seems to me that
the bird would have been safer in your own possession. However, I
can feel for your affection for your father and mother, and I
think it is just possible that I can provide a means by which
the family honour may be maintained without injury to that of
the county. So far as I am concerned, I am not interested in
Ryder's case."

"Well, I did what she said, killed the bird, and took it away with
me. On my way to Kilburn I met Peterson, the commissionaire, and
he saw me and thought I was drunk, which I may well have seemed
to be. I dropped the bird in Tottenham Court Road, and when I
picked it up again I found that a row was going on, and had to
run away without it. I never dared to go back after it, but I knew
that it would be found and that I would have news of it sooner or
later. So you see, sir, I have told you the whole truth, and I am
ready to face any consequences."

"So I did, and there was not a moment that I could call my own
until I had reached Maudsley's room. Safe inside, I took the
stone out of the goose and handed it over to him, and he made
away with it in half an hour. Well, he's got it now, or I expect
he has, and I suppose that I am in for it. That is the whole
story, sir, and as it is now in your hands, I would ask you to let
my father and mother know as gently as you could, for they have
been very good to me always and would not like anything so bad to
happen to me."

"Well, I did what she said, sir, and I took it away with me. In
the evening I went to see my friend Maudsley, and I told him
everything that had occurred. He laughed when he had heard my
story, for he knew that all those geese which went to the Alpha
were town-bred. He said that if the police only knew that I had
got away with the stone, it would be as much as my life was worth
to go and fetch it, so the best way would be to sell it, so he
would find a buyer, and we could share it between us. But just as
we were settling this, in came the police, and I had to fly. I
have never seen my friend Maudsley since, nor could I see how I
could get any money out of my stone. So I have been hiding ever
since, and I have never dared to show my face in London. Even now,
sir, I shall get seven years' penal servitude unless you can save
me, for they have my description all right, and the police are
sure to hear that I have been hanging about the market."

"So I did, and there was the bird with the stone in its crop. I
carried it home by the underground, and got out at Tottenham
Court Road. Then I went to Maudsley's, and gave him the stone. He
knew that I had not come to see him empty-handed. At first he was
frightened, but when he saw the stone he was delighted. We
planned how we should sell it, and got rid of it without the
smallest difficulty. We were both in our right minds, you
understand, and we did it as a matter of business. But now it all
comes back to me like a dream. I can hardly believe that I was
ever such a fool as to let myself be led away by a scoundrel like
Maudsley. It was Catherine Cusack who found the stone, and showed
it to me; and it was she who persuaded me to let Horner take the
blame. She'll share with me now, I suppose?"

"Well, I did what she said, Mr. Holmes, and I carried the bird
all the way to Kilburn. I told my pal what I had done, for he was
a man that it was easy to tell a thing like that to. He laughed
until he choked, and we got a knife and opened the goose. My
heart turned to water, for there was no sign of the stone, and I
knew that some terrible mistake had occurred. I left the bird,
rushed back to my sister's, and hurried into the back yard. There
was not a bird to be seen there.

"'Where are they all, Maggie?' I cried.

"'Gone to the dealer's, Jem.'

"'Which dealer's?'

"'Breckinridge, of Covent Garden.'

"'But was there another with a barred tail?' I asked, 'the same
as the one I chose?'

"'Yes, Jem; there were two barred-tailed ones, and I could never
tell them apart.'

"And that," said Holmes, turning to me with a smile, "is how a
Christmas goose saved the life of a plumber, and nearly got him
himself into trouble with the police.  The moral of the story,
Watson, is that if you would keep your secrets, you should not
tell them to a goose."
"And that's the end of it," said Holmes, resuming his seat with a
smile. "I think that I may say that that little incident is now
closed. Horner, of course, was released, though I'm afraid that
Ryder's confession will not clear him entirely. It is a most
remarkable case, and very instructive. I confess that I was
surprised to find that the goose was not only eaten, but that it
had actually laid an egg after it was dead. The Countess of
Morcar will have her blue carbuncle again, and I have no doubt
that she will be as happy to have it as she was unhappy to lose
it. You know, Watson, I am always amused when people describe my
methods as unscientific. They say that it is only through
science that the truth can be attained. But I contend that with
a little observation and with a little deduction the most
extraordinary secrets can be brought to light."
"Now, Watson," said Holmes, turning to me, "we have had some
interesting hours, but I think that I am justified in saying
that they have not been wasted. The game is played. It is a
singular thing, Watson, how a trifling incident may have such a
far-reaching influence upon the lives of men. The loss of one
goose out of a flock of twenty-four seems but a small
matter, but it made a great difference in the life of James Ryder.
The whole chain of events is linked together with extraordinary
perfection."  He smiled, and then added, "The Countess will get
her stone, Horner will be released from prison, and our good
friend Breckinridge will perhaps acquire a better knowledge of
geese than he now possesses. A case, Watson, which illustrates
better than most the value of accurate observation, and of
logical deduction from a small fact. Let us proceed to dinner."
“And now, Watson,” said Holmes, turning to me, his face ablaze
with excitement, “the game is afoot.  It appears that the
Countess’s blue carbuncle has been recovered, and the true culprit,
James Ryder, has been exposed.  Horner, the plumber, is innocent,
and we must see to clearing his name.  A most interesting case,
Watson, a most interesting case!”
"And that's the end of it," said Holmes, turning to me.  "I
think that we have done well to-night.  It's a curious case--a
most singular case--but the true culprit is, of course, James
Ryder, and I have no doubt that with the help of his confession
and this stone the matter can be easily cleared up.  Horner will
be released and the Countess will have her precious stone back.  A
goose with a blue carbuncle inside it is a most unusual sort of
Christmas present, but I think we can safely say that this
particular Christmas will be memorable for quite some time!"
"After all, Watson," said Holmes, reaching up his hand for his
clay pipe, "I am not retained by the police to supply their
deficiencies. If Horner were in danger it would be another thing;
but this fellow will not appear against him, and the case must
collapse. I suppose that I am commuting a felony, but it is just
possible that I am saving a soul. This fellow will not go wrong
again; he is too terribly frightened. Send him to gaol now, and
you make him a gaol-bird for life. Besides, it is the season of
forgiveness. Chance has put in our way a most singular and
whimsical problem, and its solution is its own reward. If you
will have the goodness to touch the bell, Doctor, we will begin
another investigation, in which, also a bird will be the chief
feature."
